title: Persistent Demo-Pool Poisoning Attacks on Online LLM Log Parsers

contributions.purpose: Identify a new security vulnerability in online LLM log parsers that use self-generated in-context learning.
contributions.mechanism: Show that the monotonically growing, never-purged demonstration pool of self-generated ICL (SG-ICL) systems like AdaParser creates a persistent attack surface that an adversary can corrupt via crafted log injection.
contributions.evaluation: Conceptual identification; grounded in AdaParser's design where entries are never purged or revalidated.
contributions.source_quote: We identify a fundamental security vulnerability in online LLM log parsers that use self-generated ICL: the monotonically growing demo pool creates a persistent attack surface.

contributions.purpose: Design a concrete attack that exploits the SG-ICL vulnerability.
contributions.mechanism: Over-generalization attack: craft log entries that replace static tokens with variable-looking values (e.g., 'node-1' -> 'node-abc123') so the LLM emits over-generalized templates with excessive wildcards, propagating through two damage channels: ICL contamination (poisoned demos retrieved via LCS similarity) and trie poisoning (over-generalized templates cached in the parsing trie).
contributions.evaluation: Implemented on AdaParser with GPT-4o-mini (temp 0), k=3 demos; evaluated against clean (C0) and random-noise control (C2).
contributions.domain: Adversarial attacks on online log parsing (AdaParser)
contributions.source_quote: We design an over-generalization attack strategy that exploits this vulnerability through two damage channels: ICL contamination and trie poisoning.

contributions.purpose: Demonstrate the attack's severity and persistence under a low budget.
contributions.mechanism: Inject 60 crafted log entries (3% of a 2000-log stream) within the first 600 logs, then measure parsing quality in a late evaluation window (logs 1500-1999), 900+ entries after injection ends.
contributions.evaluation: 40.33pp FTA drop on BGL (0.753->0.349) and 13.33pp on Thunderbird (0.400->0.267); PA drops of 80.67pp (BGL) and 49.00pp (Thunderbird); random noise control causes negligible change (-1.50pp BGL, +2.83pp Thunderbird). Averaged over 3 seeds.
contributions.source_quote: We demonstrate that injecting only 60 log entries (3% of stream) causes severe, persistent degradation: 40.33pp FTA drop on BGL and 13.33pp on Thunderbird, with damage persisting 900+ logs after injection ends.

contributions.purpose: Identify which internal mechanism drives the persistent damage.
contributions.mechanism: Ablation studies on BGL: disable SG-ICL updates after injection, and vary k (3 vs 5) demonstrations, isolating trie poisoning from demo-pool accumulation.
contributions.evaluation: Trie poisoning dominates: disabling SG-ICL barely changes the drop (40.33pp with vs 41.00pp without, delta -0.67pp); FTA is k-independent (0.349 at k=3 and k=5) though contamination rate rises 12.1%->19.1%; Thunderbird shows 0% ICL contamination yet still 13.33pp FTA drop.
contributions.source_quote: We analyze the attack mechanism through ablation studies, revealing that trie poisoning dominates over demo-pool accumulation as the primary persistence pathway.

self_declared_provenance.quote: AdaParser (Wu et al., 2024) introduces Self-Generated In-Context Learning (SG-ICL), where the system maintains a candidate pool of (log, template) pairs that grows monotonically as new logs are parsed.
Unlike traditional retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) poisoning attacks that require write access to an external knowledge base, this attack exploits the system's own learning mechanism.

PoisonedRAG (Zou et al., 2024) and SecureRAG (Cheng et al., 2025) study poisoning attacks on retrieval-augmented generation systems where attackers inject malicious documents into the retrieval corpus. Our work differs from these approaches in a fundamental way: we target online systems that generate their own retrieval corpus from model outputs.
In the context of LLMs, He et al. (2024) demonstrate that poisoning ICL demonstrations can significantly degrade performance on NLP classification tasks.

notes: Random noise control (C2) sometimes slightly improves accuracy (e.g., +2.83pp FTA on Thunderbird), underscoring the effect is targeting-specific rather than generic injection noise.
